paragraphs: The paper studies sampling when a target probability distribution is known only through its unnormalized density. It connects tempering, used in Sequential Monte Carlo, with entropic mirror descent, an optimization method. This gives a mathematical explanation for how a sampling procedure can also make progress on an optimization objective.

The authors establish that tempering corresponds to entropic mirror descent on the reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. They also obtain convergence rates for the tempering iterates. From this perspective, tempering reduces that discrepancy according to Fisher–Rao geometry. Langevin dynamics provide a contrasting route: they descend a KL objective using Wasserstein-2 geometry.

The connection has practical consequences beyond reinterpreting an existing method. The authors use it to justify common Sequential Monte Carlo practices and derive adaptive tempering rules that improve on alternative benchmarks. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: an optimization viewpoint helps explain familiar sampling choices and supplies a basis for designing better ones.
icml-2024-a-connection-between-tempering.tldr: Tempering can be understood as entropic mirror descent, yielding convergence results and improved adaptive sampling rules.

paragraphs: This paper seeks efficient graph clustering under a model combining randomness with restricted adversarial changes. The starting graph has an unknown division into two communities and α random edges between them. An adversary may add edges within communities or remove edges between them. These changes are monotone: they respect the underlying division.

Earlier work gave a polynomial-time approximation for Balanced Cut, but relied on repeatedly solving expensive semidefinite programs. The authors present a near-linear-time algorithm that finds a balanced cut with O(α) crossing edges. Its running time is O(|V|^(1+o(1)) + |E|^(1+o(1))), so its computational cost grows almost linearly with the graph’s vertices and edges.

The result provides similar clustering performance with a substantially faster algorithm in this semi-random setting. The approach also yields a near-linear-time constant-factor approximation for Dasgupta’s hierarchical clustering objective under a semi-random hierarchical block model. An extension to Sparsest Cut is described as appearing feasible, rather than established as another completed result.
icml-2024-a-near-linear-time-approximati.tldr: A near-linear-time algorithm approximates balanced graph cuts under a semi-random model with restricted adversarial changes.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models route different inputs to different subnetworks, called experts. This reduces training computation, but keeping the experts available can still make deployment expensive in memory and computation. The paper studies how to remove experts after fine-tuning while retaining the accuracy needed for a downstream task.

Its pruning rule uses changes in the router during fine-tuning. Experts associated with smaller changes in the router’s L2 norm, measured relative to the pretrained model, receive higher priority for removal. The authors prove that this strategy preserves test accuracy while substantially reducing model size and computational requirements within their theoretical setting.

That guarantee is established for binary classification with a simplified mixture-of-experts architecture. The authors separately verify the method on larger vision models, including V-MoE and E³-MoE, fine-tuned on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Together, the analysis and experiments support using router changes as a principled signal for expert pruning, while keeping the scope of the proof distinct from the larger empirical demonstrations.
icml-2024-a-provably-effective-method-fo.tldr: Changes in router norms guide expert pruning, with accuracy guarantees for a simplified setting and verification on larger vision models.

paragraphs: Neural network quantization usually reduces the precision of weights and activations to lower inference costs. Reducing the precision of the accumulator, which holds intermediate sums, can improve hardware efficiency further. However, values exceeding its numerical range cause overflow and arithmetic errors that can damage model accuracy.

Accumulator-aware quantization addresses this by constraining weights during training so inference can safely use a chosen accumulator width. The authors identify two sources of unnecessary error in the existing A2Q method: an overly restrictive constraint and a suboptimal initialization procedure. They introduce a less restrictive bound that still avoids overflow, together with a new way to initialize quantized weights from pretrained floating-point models.

A2Q+ combines those improvements with weight normalization. The paper analyzes the tradeoffs introduced by accumulator constraints and reports experiments showing substantially better tradeoffs than prior methods. Its contribution is to make more effective use of the available numerical range while preserving overflow avoidance, improving the balance between reduced precision and model accuracy.
icml-2024-a2q-improving-accumulator-awar.tldr: A2Q+ improves low-precision neural networks through looser overflow-safe weight constraints and better quantized-weight initialization.

paragraphs: Training on a carefully chosen subset of data can reduce the burden of training on an entire dataset. The challenge is deciding which examples remain useful as the retained fraction changes. Existing selection methods often work best when keeping either a small or a large fraction, rather than performing competitively across both regimes.

Best Window Selection first orders examples by difficulty score, then selects a contiguous window within that ordering. Moving the window changes the mix of easy and difficult examples. This makes the selection flexible without requiring a fixed commitment to either end of the difficulty ranking. The method evaluates candidate window quality efficiently using kernel ridge regression.

The reported experiments show BWS outperforming comparison methods across a broad range of selection ratios on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The evaluations cover both training from random initialization and fine-tuning pretrained models. These results support the usefulness of choosing where to draw a subset from the difficulty ordering, alongside deciding how much data to retain.
icml-2024-bws-best-window-selection-base.tldr: BWS selects windows of difficulty-ranked examples to improve data pruning across a broad range of retained dataset sizes.

paragraphs: CogBench evaluates language models through behavioral patterns drawn from cognitive psychology. The motivation is that overall performance scores leave aspects of model behavior unexplored. Its ten behavioral measures come from seven psychology experiments, creating a way to characterize how models reason and make choices as well as how well they perform.

The authors apply the benchmark to 40 language models. They analyze the results with statistical multilevel modeling, accounting for dependencies between models that are fine-tuned versions of the same underlying model. Their findings highlight model size and reinforcement learning from human feedback as important factors in performance and alignment with human behavior.

The study also finds that the evaluated open-source models are less risk-prone than proprietary models, while code fine-tuning does not necessarily improve behavior. Prompting techniques produce different effects: chain-of-thought prompting improves probabilistic reasoning, and take-a-step-back prompting encourages model-based behavior. These results show how a behavioral benchmark can distinguish effects that a single aggregate performance score would not describe.
icml-2024-cogbench-a-large-language-mode.tldr: CogBench uses psychology experiments to characterize language-model behavior and compare the effects of model design, training, and prompting.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups vertices using positive and negative relationships. Positive edges favor putting their endpoints together, while negative edges favor separating them. The objective counts disagreements: positive edges split across clusters and negative edges kept inside a cluster. This paper studies maintaining such a grouping while vertices arrive or are randomly deleted.

The authors give an algorithm that maintains a constant-factor approximation with amortized update time polynomial in log n. Amortized time describes the cost averaged across a sequence of updates. The guarantee therefore combines an approximately good clustering with a small average maintenance cost as the vertex stream changes.

This improves on the stated vertex-stream cost obtained from an earlier edge-stream algorithm, whose update time becomes proportional to the maximum possible degree. The distinction matters because adding or removing one vertex can involve many relationships. Experiments on real-world data complement the theoretical analysis. The result specifically covers the stated insertion and random-deletion setting, making that deletion model part of the guarantee.
icml-2024-dynamic-correlation-clustering.tldr: The algorithm maintains a constant-factor correlation clustering approximation with polylogarithmic amortized updates under vertex arrivals and random deletions.

paragraphs: Embodied agents need to make timely decisions while operating on devices with limited capacity. DeDer addresses this by transferring reasoning capabilities from a large language model into policies built with small language models. The aim is to make complex task planning practical on ordinary devices while retaining useful reasoning from the larger model.

The framework separates decision-making into a reasoning policy and a planning policy. The reasoning policy learns from data produced through an LLM’s embodied in-context learning and self-verification, and generates rationales. The planning policy uses those rationales to produce plans efficiently. Small language models can implement both parts of this hierarchy.

DeDer also introduces an embodied knowledge graph to improve intermediate rationales and uses a contrastively prompted attention model to generate multiple rationales in one inference. On the ALFRED benchmark, it surpasses leading language-planning and distillation approaches. These experiments support the applicability and efficiency of its distilled policies, showing how separating reasoning from planning can help bring LLM-derived capabilities to smaller systems.
icml-2024-embodied-cot-distillation-from.tldr: DeDer distills LLM reasoning into small reasoning and planning policies for efficient embodied agents on ordinary devices.

paragraphs: Forecasting related time series can benefit from knowing how the series connect. Hierarchical relationships add another requirement: predictions at different levels must satisfy shared constraints. This paper develops a graph-based forecasting approach that brings ordinary relationships between series and hierarchical constraints into the same learning architecture.

The method represents these dependencies in a pyramidal graph, with each layer corresponding to a hierarchy level. Trainable graph pooling operators allow the hierarchy itself to be learned when it is not supplied beforehand. Consequently, the resulting clusters are shaped by the forecasting objective, connecting the choice of groups directly to the predictions the model must make.

A differentiable reconciliation stage incorporates hierarchical constraints into the architecture and uses them to regularize predictions during learning. This connects forecasting, grouping, and consistency within one trainable system. Simulations on representative datasets compare favorably with the state of the art. The findings support learning useful hierarchical structure alongside forecasting when that structure is not already available as prior knowledge.
icml-2024-graph-based-time-series-cluste.tldr: A trainable pyramidal graph learns time-series groups and forecasts while incorporating hierarchical consistency constraints.

paragraphs: Privacy guarantees for differentially private stochastic gradient descent depend on how training batches are sampled. Practical implementations commonly use shuffling, whereas well-developed privacy analyses often assume Poisson subsampling. The paper examines the consequences of using an analysis for one sampling procedure to describe an implementation using the other.

The authors study Adaptive Batch Linear Queries, a mechanism through which the usual DP-SGD privacy analysis can be understood by post-processing. They demonstrate that its privacy guarantees can differ substantially between shuffling and Poisson subsampling. This directly challenges the practice of treating the two sampling schemes as interchangeable when reporting privacy parameters.

The mismatch arises from a practical tension: shuffling has been difficult to analyze even numerically, while Poisson sampling has strong accounting tools but is challenging to implement scalably. The result establishes that a substantial gap can occur, rather than claiming that every shuffled implementation suffers the same discrepancy. Its implication is that reported privacy guarantees require careful attention to the batch-sampling procedure actually used.
icml-2024-how-private-are-dp-sgd-impleme.tldr: Privacy analyses for Poisson-sampled DP-SGD can differ substantially from those for shuffled batches, challenging a common implementation-accounting mismatch.

paragraphs: Token-based world models represent an agent’s experience as sequences of discrete symbols, with each observation occupying several tokens. During imagined experience, generating the next observation one token at a time creates a bottleneck. The paper connects that sequential process to long training times, poor GPU utilization, and restrictions on representations.

Parallel Observation Prediction addresses the bottleneck by adding a new forward mode to a Retentive Network, tailored to reinforcement learning. The mechanism changes how observations are predicted during imagination. The authors incorporate it into REM, the Retentive Environment Model, creating an agent designed to make imagined experience substantially faster to produce.

REM achieves 15.4 times faster imagination than prior token-based world models in the reported comparison. It also reaches superhuman performance on 12 of the 26 Atari 100K games while training in less than 12 hours. The speedup specifically concerns imagination, while the benchmark results show the resulting agent’s task performance. Together, they support parallel observation prediction as a practical way to reduce a major world-model bottleneck.
icml-2024-improving-token-based-world-mo.tldr: REM uses parallel observation prediction to accelerate imagination 15.4-fold and achieve superhuman results on 12 Atari 100K games.

paragraphs: Error-correcting codes help recover information sent through noisy communication channels. Designing effective linear block codes that are also efficiently decodable is especially important for short blocks. Although neural decoders have shown advantages, learning the code itself remains difficult. This paper proposes jointly training the encoder and decoder for binary linear block codes.

The authors adapt the coding setup to permit efficient, differentiable optimization over the two-element Galois field, the algebraic setting for binary codes. They also introduce a Transformer whose attention mask is differentiable. This allows gradients associated with the code to propagate through the model, supporting an end-to-end learning process.

The reported findings cover both decoding and code design. The decoder improves on existing neural decoders for conventional codes, and the learned codes outperform analogous conventional ones. Those learned codes also improve performance with traditional decoding methods. This final result matters because it shows that the benefits extend beyond pairing the codes with the particular neural decoder used to develop them.
icml-2024-learning-linear-block-error-co.tldr: Joint differentiable training learns binary linear codes and a Transformer decoder, with learned-code gains also extending to traditional decoders.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling makes contextual-bandit decisions using samples from a posterior distribution that changes as observations arrive. Drawing those samples exactly is usually intractable. Approximate inference offers a route forward, but the paper identifies a tradeoff: some approximations estimate the posterior poorly, while others require expensive computation at each decision round.

VITS uses Gaussian variational inference to build a posterior approximation that is efficient to compute and easy to sample from. This makes approximate inference part of the decision-making algorithm itself. The approach aims to retain the benefits of posterior-based exploration without making each round depend on costly sampling procedures.

For linear contextual bandits, the authors prove a sublinear regret bound with the same order of dependence on dimension and number of rounds as traditional Thompson sampling. Sublinear regret means accumulated decision loss grows more slowly than the interaction horizon. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets further demonstrate effectiveness, combining a computationally practical approximation with a theoretical guarantee in the linear setting.
icml-2024-mathttvits-variational-inferen.tldr: VITS uses Gaussian variational inference for efficient Thompson sampling and matches its regret order for linear contextual bandits.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often has access to several data sources, each providing a different graph view. The paper formalizes this situation through a family of multi-view stochastic block models. This supplies a mathematical setting for studying how multiple graphs can contribute to recovering community structure and what algorithms can achieve from the available information.

The authors first analyze efficient methods that combine the graphs by taking their union. They then introduce an efficient algorithm that examines each graph’s structure separately. Under the proposed model, this algorithm provably outperforms earlier approaches. The result establishes a benefit from retaining information about individual views during analysis.

The paper also gives an information-theoretic lower bound, addressing limits imposed by the model rather than just the speed or design of a particular algorithm. This complements the positive algorithmic result with a statement about what is achievable at all. Together, the model, algorithm, and lower bound provide a theoretical basis for understanding the value and limits of multiple graph sources.
icml-2024-multi-view-stochastic-block-mo.tldr: A new multi-view graph model supports an efficient clustering algorithm that provably benefits from analyzing graph views separately.

paragraphs: Music generation is difficult to evaluate because listeners can interpret the same text request differently and value different musical qualities. MusicRL addresses this by fine-tuning the pretrained MusicLM generator with reinforcement learning. The model generates discrete audio tokens, and training uses rewards assigned to complete sequences.

The authors develop two approaches. MusicRL-R uses reward functions focused on text adherence and audio quality, designed with help from selected raters. MusicRL-U learns from 300,000 pairwise preferences collected from users of the deployed MusicLM system. This second approach brings large-scale listener feedback directly into the fine-tuning process.

Human evaluations prefer both versions to the baseline, and MusicRL-RU, which combines the approaches, receives the strongest preference among the evaluated models. Ablation studies indicate that matching the text and producing high-quality audio explain only part of what listeners prefer. The findings support continued involvement of human listeners in training, because explicit quality criteria capture only some of the subjective judgments involved in musical appreciation.
icml-2024-musicrl-aligning-music-generat.tldr: MusicRL improves listener preference through reinforcement learning that combines quality-focused rewards with large-scale human feedback.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching pairs arriving vertices with available vertices on the other side of a graph. Decisions are judged against an optimal algorithm that sees the entire instance beforehand. This paper studies whether external advice can improve performance while preserving protection against bad advice, for unweighted matching with equally sized vertex sets.

Under adversarial arrival order, the authors prove a sharp incompatibility: no learning-augmented method can be both 1-consistent and more than 1/2-robust. Here, 1-consistency means matching the offline optimum with correct advice, while robustness describes the guarantee when advice is unreliable. This tradeoff holds even though the advice-free RANKING algorithm guarantees 1−1/e, exceeding one half.

Random arrival order permits a more favorable result. Using distribution-testing methods, the authors design an algorithm whose competitive guarantee varies with advice quality, interpolating between any ratio attainable without advice and the optimal ratio of one. The contrast shows that arrival assumptions fundamentally affect how much an algorithm can benefit from predictions while retaining a fallback guarantee.
icml-2024-online-bipartite-matching-with.tldr: Advice faces a consistency–robustness barrier under adversarial arrivals, but random arrivals permit guarantees that improve with advice quality.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle to carry information over long distances when graph bottlenecks force many signals through limited representations. This problem is called over-squashing. Existing approaches often change graph connections to improve information propagation, but those changes alter the original topology and may distort how information flows.

PANDA takes a different architectural approach by selectively increasing the width of node representations. It targets nodes with high centrality, which can be potential sources of over-squashing. Giving these nodes larger hidden states lets them hold more of the information arriving from distant parts of the graph as message passing proceeds.

Experiments show PANDA outperforming existing graph-rewiring methods in the reported evaluations. The findings suggest that increasing representation capacity at selected nodes can be a compelling alternative to modifying graph connectivity. The central contribution is to connect where information accumulates with how much representational space a node receives, addressing the bottleneck through node capacity while respecting the graph’s original structure.
icml-2024-panda-expanded-width-aware-mes.tldr: PANDA mitigates graph information bottlenecks by widening selected node representations and outperforms rewiring methods in reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies a differential-privacy framework that first adds noise to an input and then projects the noisy result back into the set of admissible datasets. Projection enforces the structural restrictions of that set. The authors use this framework to develop efficient algorithms for releasing useful summaries of sensitive data.

One contribution is private release of pairwise cosine similarities. Another is an algorithm for k-way marginal queries over n features, extending comparable guarantees beyond the even values of k handled by prior work. The authors also address t-sparse datasets and obtain stronger guarantees when t is at most n^(5/6)/log n.

The analysis uses tight sum-of-squares certificates to bound the Gaussian complexity of relevant solution sets. These technical bounds support the privacy framework’s guarantees and provide a theoretical explanation for why fast input-perturbation algorithms can work well in practice. The contribution combines new private-release algorithms with analysis explaining how admissible structure and sparsity can improve what these algorithms achieve.
icml-2024-perturb-and-project-differenti.tldr: Adding noise and projecting onto admissible datasets yields efficient private similarity and marginal-query algorithms with improved sparse-data guarantees.

paragraphs: Language models learn from text containing many different personality traits and behavioral preferences. This paper asks how to elicit a chosen persona from that variety. It formalizes persona elicitation as a task in which the model’s behavior should align with a specified target, making behavioral customization an explicit objective.

Persona In-Context Learning, or PICLe, approaches that objective through Bayesian inference. Its central mechanism is a likelihood-ratio criterion for choosing in-context examples. Those examples provide guidance within the prompt, and the criterion is designed to select examples that optimally steer the model toward the desired persona.

The authors evaluate PICLe against baseline methods across three language models and report evidence of its effectiveness. The contribution links a formal account of persona elicitation to a concrete example-selection strategy. This matters because the prompt examples become a deliberate tool for shaping behavioral preferences, with a selection rule grounded in the target persona and an empirical evaluation across multiple models.
icml-2024-picle-eliciting-diverse-behavi.tldr: PICLe uses a Bayesian likelihood-ratio criterion to select prompt examples that steer language models toward a target persona.

paragraphs: Imaging inverse problems reconstruct images from degraded or incomplete observations. This paper uses text-to-image latent diffusion models as image priors for that reconstruction. Existing approaches often use an empty text prompt, which the authors identify as a source of potentially suboptimal performance.

P2L tunes the text embedding while reverse diffusion is running. Its unified optimization framework considers the prompt representation, latent values, and pixel values together, updating them through alternating minimization. Adapting the prompt during reconstruction helps generated images remain more faithful to the diffusion prior and substantially reduces artifacts associated with using latent diffusion for these problems.

The reported evaluations show P2L outperforming inverse-problem solvers based on both pixel-space and latent-space diffusion across tasks including super-resolution, deblurring, and inpainting. The method also demonstrates scaling to higher resolutions without artifacts in the reported results. The contribution makes text conditioning an actively optimized part of reconstruction, connecting prompt adaptation with improvements in image quality and the use of higher-resolution diffusion priors.
icml-2024-prompt-tuning-latent-diffusion.tldr: P2L tunes text embeddings during diffusion-based image reconstruction to reduce artifacts and improve results across several inverse problems.

paragraphs: Pretraining on multiple tasks often produces features that support later adaptation by changing only a final linear layer. This paper provides a theoretical explanation for feature learning in nonlinear networks trained across tasks. It studies two-layer ReLU networks, extending beyond prior theory focused on single-task training or linear models.

The key insight is that multitask pretraining induces a pseudo-contrastive loss: it encourages representations to align points that tend to share labels across tasks. The analysis assumes binary classification tasks whose labels depend on an r-dimensional projection of data from a much larger d-dimensional input space. Under this setting, a simple gradient-based algorithm recovers the relevant projection.

The recovered representation supports downstream generalization with sample and neuron complexity independent of the ambient dimension d. In contrast, with high probability over a single task’s draw, training only on that task cannot guarantee recovery of all r underlying features. The result explains how task diversity can reveal shared structure that a single task may leave insufficiently identified.
icml-2024-provable-multi-task-representa.tldr: Under a shared low-dimensional task structure, multitask training provably recovers features that support dimension-independent downstream learning.

paragraphs: Probabilistic regression forecasts describe uncertainty about future outputs. When several output dimensions depend on one another, checking or adjusting each dimension separately can be misleading and even harmful. This paper addresses uncertainty jointly, focusing on predictive distributions represented by samples rather than treating output coordinates as separate forecasting problems.

The authors define calibration using highest density regions, which describe portions of the joint distribution where probability is concentrated. Their recalibration method accounts for dependencies across output dimensions and produces samples satisfying this HDR calibration criterion. The theoretical claim is tied to that specific notion of calibration.

Evaluations examine both the method’s performance and the quality of its recalibrated samples. They include multidimensional regression benchmarks, plasma dynamics during nuclear fusion reactions, and demand forecasting used for decision-making. These applications connect joint uncertainty estimation with practical settings where relationships between outputs matter. The contribution supplies a sample-based adjustment procedure and a corresponding calibration guarantee for assessing its output.
icml-2024-sampling-based-multi-dimension.tldr: A sample-based recalibration method accounts for dependencies between outputs and guarantees calibration under a highest-density-region criterion.

paragraphs: Editing video with a pretrained image diffusion model requires maintaining consistency as the scene changes over time. Many methods explicitly match pixels or features between frames, but strong nonrigid motion makes those correspondences difficult. Slicedit approaches the problem using the visual structure found in slices through space and time.

The key observation is that spatiotemporal slices of natural videos share characteristics with natural images. A text-to-image model can therefore act as a prior on those slices as well as on ordinary video frames. Slicedit processes both spatial and spatiotemporal slices, using the same kind of image model to support appearance editing and temporal consistency.

The method produces text-guided edits while retaining the original video’s structure and motion. Extensive experiments across real-world videos show advantages over existing baselines in the reported evaluations. The contribution demonstrates a way to reuse pretrained image-generation capabilities across a video’s time dimension, making the representation of the video itself central to preserving consistency during editing.
icml-2024-slicedit-zero-shot-video-editi.tldr: Slicedit applies an image diffusion model to video frames and spatiotemporal slices to produce text-guided edits with consistent motion.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves nested optimization problems, raising the question of whether nesting necessarily worsens sample complexity relative to a single optimization level. This paper addresses that question through SPABA, a single-loop stochastic algorithm adapted from the PAGE method for nonconvex optimization.

The authors prove that SPABA achieves optimal sample complexity in both finite-sum and expectation settings. Their analysis shows no complexity gap between stochastic bilevel and single-level optimization when PAGE is used. The scope of that statement matters: the paper notes that a gap may exist in analyses using other gradient estimators, including SGD and SAGA.

The authors also derive additional single-loop bilevel algorithms whose sample-complexity guarantees match or improve the state of the art. Numerical experiments show superior practical performance for the proposed methods. The combined contribution links an optimal theoretical result to algorithm design, demonstrating that the choice of stochastic estimator can be central to whether nested optimization incurs an additional complexity burden.
icml-2024-spaba-a-single-loop-and-probab.tldr: SPABA achieves optimal stochastic bilevel sample complexity, matching single-level complexity when using the PAGE estimator.

paragraphs: Deep-learning optimizers balance cheap gradient-based updates against potentially more informative curvature-based updates. Second-order methods often also need stabilizing rules, such as damping, to work effectively. This paper asks how much those rules contribute to performance independently of the curvature model they usually accompany.

The authors study AdamQLR, which combines Adam’s update directions with damping and learning-rate selection techniques from K-FAC. Viewing Adam through a second-order perspective motivates this combination. It provides a way to investigate the usefulness of K-FAC’s adaptive heuristics when attached to a different source of update directions.

Experiments cover regression and classification tasks at different scales and use different hyperparameter-tuning methodologies. The findings are mixed: K-FAC’s adaptive heuristics vary in their standalone effectiveness. Nevertheless, an untuned AdamQLR configuration can achieve performance-versus-runtime comparable to tuned benchmarks. This supports examining stabilization and step selection as meaningful contributors to optimizer behavior, while preserving the finding that their benefits are variable across the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-studying-k-fac-heuristics-by-v.tldr: AdamQLR combines Adam updates with K-FAC heuristics, finding variable benefits but competitive performance-versus-runtime without tuning in one configuration.
